title: Bistability, Bubbling Dynamics and Optimal Control of Soil-Borne Plant Fungal Disease
content: In this article, a mathematical model for soil-borne fungal disease in plants, where the disease transmission occurs due to interactions of susceptible plants with fungal pathogens existing in the soil, is developed and analyzed in terms of positivity, boundedness, equilibria and their stability, to explore conditions under which the disease can be effectively controlled. The condition of existence and direction of Hopf bifurcation are analytically found using normal form theory and then verified numerically. In addition, optimal control analysis is carried out by introducing time-dependent controls such as cultural control, fungicides and biological control in the model. The necessary optimality conditions are obtained using Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle. This study shows that the infection transmission rate, growth of fungus in the soil and pathogen amplification rate are among the significant parameters affecting the spread of disease. Plant-free equilibrium is stable when Also, disease-pressure index is less than unity. It is also found that the endemic equilibrium undergoes subcritical and supercritical Hopf bifurcations as well as bubbling. Finally, it is observed that the suggested optimal control approach has the ability to minimize the number of infected plants and density of soil-borne fungal pathogens.
